content: A disabled millennial writer reflects on feeling unusually lucky just to leave the house, highlighting how basic social activities like going to work, seeing friends, or meeting anyone at all can no longer be taken for granted for many disabled people. Citing new research from disability charity Scope, they note that nearly half of working-age disabled people in Britain—around 3 million—report feeling “always or often” lonely, revealing a severe, chronic isolation. This sits within a wider national problem, as official statistics already label Britain the “loneliness capital of Europe,” with weaker social ties than other EU countries and young people particularly affected, but the data suggest that disabled people are experiencing a distinct and acute epidemic of loneliness.
